questions.q: When a positively charged body is brought near an insulated, uncharged conductor, charging by induction produces a net force of attraction. Why?
options: Electrons are stripped off the conductor, leaving it positively charged so it repels the body
The positively charged body attracts electrons in the conductor, so the near end gains an excess of electrons (negative) and is attracted more strongly than the far positive end is repelled
The conductor must touch the charged body for any induced charges to form
Induced charges give the conductor the same sign as the charging body, producing repulsion
questions.explanation: The positively charged body attracts electrons to the near end (an excess of electrons, negatively charged) while the far end has a deficiency of electrons (positively charged). Because the negative induced charges are closer, the attraction outweighs the repulsion, giving a net force of attraction. Induction acts without contact and is the odd one out among the charging methods.

questions.q: Coulomb's Law states that the force between two charges at rest is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to what?
options: The distance between them
The square of the distance between them
The sum of the charges
The square root of the distance between them
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law: F is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance, r. Coulomb himself showed that halving each charge cut the force to a quarter, and the inverse-square on distance means halving r multiplies the force by four. Forgetting to square the distance factor is the classic error.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the electric field at a point 30 cm from a point charge of \(+2.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}\)? Use \(E = kQ/r^2\) with \(k = 9.0 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}\).
working: \(E = 2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}\), directed away from the positive charge
questions.explanation: Direct application of \(E = kQ/r^2\), exactly the textbook sample problem. The field points away from a positive charge. Note this is the field of a point charge; between parallel plates you instead use \(E = V/d\).

questions.q: Electric current is a measure of the rate of flow of charge around a circuit. Which equation expresses this, and what is the SI unit of current?
options: \(I = Q/t\), measured in amperes
\(I = Qt\), measured in coulombs
\(I = t/Q\), measured in volts
\(Q = I/t\), measured in amperes
questions.explanation: Current is the quantity of charge Q flowing past a point in time t, so \(I = Q/t\), measured in amperes. One ampere is the current when one coulomb of charge passes a point each second. Current is about flow (charge per second), not energy.

questions.q: Ohm established experimentally that the current I in a metal wire is proportional to the voltage drop V across it. Which statement correctly describes Ohm's Law?
options: \(V = IR\), where R is numerically equal to the constant gradient of the straight V–I line
\(V = I/R\), and the graph of V versus I is a curve for all conductors
\(R = VI\), where R increases as the current increases
\(V = I + R\), where R is the area under the V–I graph
questions.explanation: Plotting V versus I for an ohmic metal wire gives a straight line, and \(V = IR\) where the resistance R is the constant gradient. A component is ohmic when this graph is straight; a filament lamp is non-ohmic because its resistance rises as it heats, curving the graph.

questions.q: A toaster is labelled '240 V, 800 W'. Using \(P = VI\), calculate its normal operating current.
questions.explanation: Rearranging \(P = VI\) gives \(I = P/V = 800/240 = 3.3\,\mathrm{A}\), the textbook sample value. The resistance could then be found from \(R = V^2/P = 240^2/800 = 72\,\Omega\). Choosing the power formula that matches the quantities given is the key exam reflex.

questions.q: For resistors connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the effective resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances. What does this tell you about the effective resistance?
options: It equals the sum of the individual resistances
It is always less than the smallest individual resistance
It equals the largest individual resistance
It is the average of the individual resistances
questions.explanation: Adding resistors in parallel adds more paths for the current to flow, so it is easier for current to flow and the effective resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance. Remember to take the reciprocal at the end when computing the parallel value.

questions.q: From memory: for devices connected in series versus in parallel, which quantity (current or voltage) is the same, and which is shared?
keyPoints: Devices in series have the same current and share the voltage between them.
Devices in parallel have the same voltage and the current is shared between them.
These rules still apply even when the circuit contains non-ohmic devices.
questions.explanation: If you recalled 'series: same current, voltage shared' and 'parallel: same voltage, current shared', grade yourself Good or Easy. Stating which quantity is constant and which divides for each is exactly what earns the marks.

questions.q: A wire carries a conventional current towards the right of the page. By the right-hand grip rule, what is the direction of the magnetic field directly above and directly below the wire?
options: Out of the page both above and below
Out of the page above the wire and into the page below the wire
Into the page above the wire and out of the page below the wire
Into the page both above and below
questions.explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb pointing right along the conventional current, the fingers curl out of the page above the wire and into the page below it. The field forms complete circles around the wire. Getting this direction right is a recurring exam mark and underpins the motor effect next year.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of domains, how a ferromagnetic material such as iron becomes magnetised when placed in a magnetic field.
keyPoints: A ferromagnetic material is made up of many magnetic domains; within each domain nearly all the atomic magnets are lined up in the same direction.
When unmagnetised, the domains point in random directions so there is no overall magnetism.
Placed in an external magnetic field, the domains line up in the direction of the field; when all are aligned the material is fully magnetised (saturated), giving a strong net field.
questions.explanation: The marks are for: domains as small aligned regions, random orientation cancelling out, and the domains lining up with an external field to add together. Naming the domains and the random-to-aligned change is the difference between bands.

questions.q: Kirchhoff's two circuit laws each express a conservation principle. Which law expresses conservation of energy?
options: The current law: the currents into a junction equal the currents out
The voltage law: the voltages around a loop sum to zero
Ohm's law: V = IR around the loop
Coulomb's law: the force depends on the product of the charges
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff's current law (currents in = currents out at a junction) is conservation of charge; Kirchhoff's voltage law (voltages around a loop sum to zero, supply equalling the total of the drops) is conservation of energy. Naming the conservation principle behind each law is the point students most often drop.
